q: How do you stay professional when you are frustrated at work?
ans: Describe a real routine: pause before responding, separate the problem from the person, take a short break if needed, and raise the issue calmly with facts. Show that you vent through appropriate channels and do not take frustration out on teammates. Illustrative example (use your own): 'When [situation] frustrated me, I stepped away briefly, wrote down the facts, and discussed it with [person] in a calm manner, which solved it.'
fu: Tell me about a time you lost your temper.
How do you react when a colleague is frustrated with you?

q: What does being reliable mean to you, and how do you demonstrate it?
ans: Define reliability as doing what you commit to, on time, and communicating early when something changes. Support with habits such as realistic estimates, regular updates, and double-checking deliverables, plus one real example. Illustrative example (use your own): 'In [project] I committed to [task] by [date], told the team early when I hit a blocker, and delivered with their help.'
fu: What do you do when you cannot meet a commitment?
How do you estimate your work?

q: If nobody assigns you any work in your first week, what would you do?
ans: Show structured initiative: ask your manager or buddy for priorities, read documentation and the codebase or process materials, set up your environment, observe team meetings, and pick up small tasks or onboarding exercises. Communicate what you are doing so you do not appear idle. Illustrative example (adapt): 'I would ask my manager what to focus on, study the documentation and recent work, ask teammates for small tasks, and share a short summary of what I learned.'
cm: Starting unrelated work without telling anyone
fu: How would you choose a first task?
How would you handle it if the quiet period continued for weeks?

q: What are you doing right now to prepare for this role?
ans: Describe concrete, current preparation: specific skills you are practising, projects in progress, courses completed, mock interviews, and reading about the company's domain. Show that your preparation matches the job description. Illustrative example (use your real activities): 'I am strengthening [skill] by building [small project], practising [topic] regularly, and studying how [domain] works.'
cm: Claiming skills you are not building
fu: What gap are you working on most?
How do you measure your progress?

q: What first got you interested in technology, and how has that interest developed?
ans: Share an honest origin, such as a project, a subject you enjoyed, or a problem you wanted to solve, and trace how it grew through courses, projects, and practice into your current direction. Keep it genuine and concise. Illustrative example (replace with your story): 'It started when [real event]. I then explored [skill], built [project], and that led me to focus on [area].'
fu: What keeps you curious now?
What has disappointed you about the field?

q: What makes a company a good place to work, in your view?
ans: Mention factors such as learning opportunities, mentorship, respectful culture, transparent communication, and meaningful work. Show that you value contribution and not just perks. Where possible, link to how you have seen those qualities in practice. Illustrative example (use your values): 'For me it is a place where people learn from each other, feedback is honest, and work has clear purpose. I try to contribute that kind of culture myself.'
fu: How would you recognise a poor culture?
How do you contribute to a team's culture?

q: If you are not selected for this role, what will you do next?
ans: Show maturity: you would ask for feedback, work on the gaps, and continue applying, while making clear this role is a strong preference. Do not sound defeated or entitled. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'I would be disappointed, since I want this role, but I would ask for feedback, strengthen my gaps, and keep improving. I would also be glad to be considered for future openings.'
fu: What feedback would be most useful?
How would you stay motivated after repeated rejections?

q: Which skill required for this role are you weakest in, and how will you close the gap?
ans: Name a real gap by comparing the job description with your skills, and give a specific plan with a timeline: resources, practice projects, and mentoring. Show that you can become productive despite the gap. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'The role mentions [skill] and I am still developing in it. I am studying [resource], building [small project], and I plan to be comfortable with it within [realistic time].'
cm: Naming an essential skill with no plan
fu: How will you prioritise it against other learning?
Who could help you with it?

q: What is the difference between a job and a career for you?
ans: Explain that a job is a role you perform while a career is a long-term path of growing skills and responsibility, and say you are looking for the latter. Link it to your plan for learning and contribution. Illustrative example (use your own view): 'A job pays for current work; a career builds over years. I want a place where each role prepares me for the next and I can keep growing.'
fu: How will this job contribute to your career?
What would a bad career decision look like?

q: Do you plan to pursue higher studies such as an M.Tech, MS, or MBA?
ans: Be honest but clear about your immediate commitment. If you have no current plan, say you are focused on building experience. If you may study later, say it is a long-term possibility and that you would discuss it with the company, not abruptly leave. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'My focus now is starting my career and building skills. If I ever consider further study, it would be a considered long-term decision, and I would discuss it openly.'
cm: Saying you will study soon and sound uncommitted
fu: Would you pursue it while working?
What would change your mind?

q: Are you comfortable with a role that involves direct interaction with clients?
ans: Express willingness and explain your approach: listen carefully, communicate clearly, be honest about limitations, and escalate when needed. Mention any real experience such as presenting a project or helping users. If you are less experienced, show a plan to develop it. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'Yes. I would listen carefully, confirm requirements, and be honest about timelines. I have presented [real project], and I am building this skill further.'
fu: How would you handle an angry client?
What would you do if a client asked for something impossible?

q: Are you comfortable with travel or onsite assignments that may last several months?
ans: Answer truthfully and practically. If you are open, say so and mention readiness for adjusting to new places. If you have constraints, discuss them respectfully and ask about notice periods, duration, and support. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'Yes, I am open to it for project needs. I would like to know the usual notice period and duration, and I can plan accordingly.'
fu: What would make it difficult?
How would you adjust to a new place?

q: How would you work with a manager who is younger or less technically experienced than you?
ans: Show maturity: a manager's role is direction, prioritisation, and removing blockers, not necessarily being the best coder. Describe respecting their authority, sharing your expertise constructively, and giving input through facts. Avoid arrogance. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'I would respect their role and support their goals, share technical views clearly with reasoning, and accept decisions even when I disagree. I would learn what they do well.'
cm: Saying age does not matter without explaining
fu: What if their instruction is technically wrong?
What do you look for in a good manager?

q: What would a mentor or professor who knows you well say about you?
ans: Provide a balanced, credible view with one strength and one growth area, ideally based on actual feedback. Name the mentor's context so the answer feels real. Illustrative example (use real feedback): 'My professor [name or role] might say I am consistent and curious about [subject], and that I should speak up more. I am working on that.'
fu: Could we contact them as a reference?
Did their feedback change what you do?

q: How would you balance family commitments with the demands of a job?
ans: Show planning and commitment: you manage your time, communicate early about important needs, and deliver reliably. Do not share excessive personal detail, and remember you may politely steer back to professional topics if the question becomes too personal. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'I plan ahead, communicate early when I need flexibility, and make sure my commitments at work are met. My family supports my career goals.'
fu: How do you prioritise when both need you?
What support helps you perform best?

q: Are you comfortable with a training period at a lower stipend before the full salary begins?
ans: Ask for clarity, show commitment, and evaluate fairly. Clarify the duration, stipend, what training covers, and what happens at the end. Express willingness if the terms are reasonable and the training is real. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'I value structured training. I would like to understand the duration, stipend, and conversion criteria, and I am open if the terms are clear.'
fu: What would a fair conversion process look like?
What would you do if the terms changed?

q: When would you be able to join if selected?
ans: Give a realistic, honest date based on your academic or notice-period situation, and mention any dependencies such as final exams or documentation. Offer flexibility where possible. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): 'I will complete my final semester on [date], so I could join by [date]. I can start earlier on a remote basis if you prefer.'
fu: What if we needed you earlier?
What documents will you need before joining?

q: How would you respond if the salary offered is lower than you expected?
ans: Stay professional: thank them, ask how the compensation is structured and how it evolves, and discuss factors such as learning and growth. If you decide to negotiate, base it on research and your value, not pressure. Be ready to decline politely if it does not work. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'I would thank you for the offer, ask about the breakdown and growth path, and discuss whether there is flexibility based on my skills. My priority is the right opportunity.'
fu: What would be a deal-breaker?
How would you decline politely?

q: How is AI changing the kind of job you are applying for, and how will you stay relevant?
ans: Show balanced awareness: AI tools can speed up routine tasks, so value shifts toward problem framing, design, testing, review, and communication. Describe how you use AI tools responsibly, verify output, and keep strengthening fundamentals. Avoid hype or fear. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'AI tools can speed up routine coding, so I focus on fundamentals, reviewing outputs carefully, and understanding the problem. I use AI assistants for [real use] while verifying the result.'
fu: Where have AI tools been wrong for you?
What would you never delegate to an AI tool?

q: What would you do if the job turned out to be different from what you expected after joining?
ans: Describe a mature process: give it time, learn why the role is structured that way, identify what is valuable, then discuss concerns with your manager and look for adjustments. Leaving should be a last resort after genuine effort. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'I would first understand the reasons, make the most of what I can learn, then discuss my aims with my manager and look for ways to align the work.'
fu: How long would you give it?
What would you say to your manager?

q: What is your biggest professional pet peeve, and how do you deal with it?
ans: Choose something mild and work-related, such as unclear communication or missed commitments, and show that you handle it constructively by clarifying expectations rather than complaining. Avoid anything that sounds like intolerance of normal people or teamwork. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'I find unclear instructions frustrating, so I clarify expectations early and confirm in writing.'
cm: Naming a strong dislike of colleagues
fu: Have you ever been the cause of this pet peeve for others?
How do you work with someone who has the habit?

q: If you could change one thing about your college education, what would it be?
ans: Give a thoughtful, constructive answer focused on your own learning, such as wanting earlier hands-on projects or more industry exposure, and explain what you have done to fill that gap yourself. Avoid blaming the institution. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'I would add more hands-on project work early on. I filled that gap by building [real project] on my own.'
kp: Action taken to fill the gap
fu: What was the most valuable course and why?
How did you fill the gap?

q: When you are stuck on a problem for hours, what do you do, and when do you ask for help?
ans: Describe a method: define the problem, try systematic debugging, search documentation, set a time limit, then ask for help with a clear description of what you tried. Show balance between independence and efficiency. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'I time-box myself to about 30 to 45 minutes, document what I tried, and then ask a teammate with a precise question. That saves everyone time.'
fu: Give an example of a problem you solved this way.
How do you choose whom to ask?

q: How do you react if someone else receives credit for work you did?
ans: Show maturity: first check the facts, then speak calmly and privately with the person or your manager, and focus on making contributions visible, not on blame. Build habits such as sharing progress updates and documenting your work. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'I would speak privately and calmly, clarify my contribution, and make my updates more visible in future so work is attributed accurately.'
cm: Saying credit does not matter at all
fu: How do you make sure teammates get credit?
What if it happened repeatedly?

q: Is there anything else you would like us to know that we have not asked?
ans: Use this as a short closing statement: restate your strongest fit for the role, mention one relevant point not yet covered, and express enthusiasm. Keep it under 30 seconds and avoid introducing new weaknesses. Illustrative example (adapt): 'Only that I am very interested in this role. I have prepared by [real action], and I would be happy to complete any assessment or share my project work.'
fu: What is the one thing you want us to remember?
How soon could you begin?
